text:
I've had a rocky experience with Linktree that raises some real concerns about how the platform is managed.

Red flag 1: About a year ago, I received two separate emails, roughly an hour apart, both informing me that my account had been unbanned. I hadn't been notified of any ban in the first place, so this was strange, though I let it slide at the time.

Red flag 2: More recently, I discovered that Signal URLs work perfectly fine in the top "Quick Links" bar, but are blocked in the main body of my Linktree page for being a "suspicious link." Signal is a well-established, widely trusted messaging app, so this inconsistency doesn't make sense. If the link is safe enough for one part of the page, why is it flagged as suspicious in another? This smells like a programming or policy oversight that nobody has bothered to fix.

Red flag 3: When I reached out to support for clarification, I was simply told that I can't post "suspicious links," without any acknowledgment of the double standard I'd pointed out. No real explanation, no fix, just a canned response.

Linktree, do better. This seems like amateur hour.

There are tons, just tons of these social link organizing apps. Other options offer better user experience, improved support, less cluttered ads in the page and forwarding emails.
title: Inconsistent moderation, mindless support

Building a page builder specifically for service businesses (tattoo artists, hairstylists, personal trainers, massage therapists).
The insight: these people don't need "websites" in the traditional sense. They need specific functional pages - a digital waiver, a booking page, an intake form, a bio link. But every existing tool (Wix, Squarespace, even Linktree) assumes you want to "design" something.
So I'm building something where you describe your business in plain text and get back a functional page in seconds. No templates to browse, no drag-and-drop, no color picker decisions.
The most interesting technical challenge has been making the AI output actually look professional without giving users any design controls. Turns out constraining the design space makes the average output much better than giving people unlimited freedom.

DayOne.fan gives artists a free hub at dayone.fan/username (replaces Linktree), track pages that double as ad landing pages, a built-in Meta Ads Manager that publishes to your own ad account, Smart Replies for DMs and comments, and fan email capture.

I got tired of trying to explain my views in Twitter threads, so I built ViewTree – it's like Linktree, but instead of links to your stuff, it's a clean page of what you actually believe, support, or oppose. No more explaining nuanced topics over and over.
Check it out: https://viewtree-test.vercel.app/
How it works:
Sign up, pick your username (viewtr.ee/@yourname)
Add "view cards" – I believe X, I support Y, I'm uncertain about Z
Drag to reorder them however you want
Customize your theme, add your bio and socials
Drop the link in your bio, or share with friends and fans
Main features:
Copy views from others – see a view you agree with on someone else's page? Click to add it to yours
Drag-and-drop ordering – arrange your views however you want
Live preview – see exactly how your public page looks as you edit
Custom themes – make it match your vibe (background, colors, font)
Different view types – "I believe," "I support," "I oppose," "I'm uncertain about," or write your own
Why I built this: People kept asking "what do you think about X?" and I had nowhere to point them. No good way to say "here's what I stand for" without writing an essay every time or maintaining a pinned thread.

As someone who has moderated multiple subreddits, and single handedly brought a subreddit from 0 to 100,00 subscribers, this misunderstands subreddits, moderation, and the relationship between Reddit and moderators. IMO subreddits were supposed to be like random forums on the internet of old, but with a shared substrate. Those forums were singularly owned as well and if you didn't like the operators you moved on, because there was no one you could escalate to.
There is fundementally a social contract between Reddit and its moderators. Moderators get autonomy and control, and reddit gets content that keeps users around. As long as Reddit does not pay moderators, autonomy and control is all they can give moderators. I'm investing a lot of effort, and I'd like to retain some control. IMO creating a community is more like starting an open source project on Github with a lot of community contributions.
If you take away autonomy and control from moderators, what is in it for the moderator? Imagine if github started seizing projects wholesale, taking them over and installing new maintainers. People would move off the platform.
Some people say that moderators are unpaid employees, but IMO that is only to the degree that moderators are required to carry out Reddit's agenda and priorities. We don't call OS maintainers github employees. I don't mind if Reddit benefits from my communities, as long as I can run it the way I want. If you take away autonomy and control, moderators absolutely become unpaid employees.
If Reddit didn't like my policies and took my subreddits, I would take that as a strong signal that Reddit is not the place to build my communities. The API debacle, protests, and mod removals caused me to decentralize my community more. I spam a linktree in my subreddit that links to Discord and other resources, exactly to protect against community seizeure by Reddit.
I think you touch on some real issues. One is of namespacing; folks can sit on valuable portions of the namespace and basically extract rent. We have the same issues for domains, and haven't solved it there. Some places like github semi-solve it by putting repo's in organizations, but that shifts the namespace issue to the organizational level.
The other problem is second generation moderators. Most moderators are terrible at succession planning, and so generally chose terrible successors. Many second generation moderators don't understand the original decisions that shaped the community, and what makes the original community successfully. Reddit should do more to encourage succession planning, and teach moderators how to do it.

Three months ago, I started building Supedia, a digital resource hub for solopreneurs, creators, and anyone building online.
The premise is simple: the internet is full of valuable PDFs, templates, eBooks, and swipe files—but they’re scattered across blogs, Gumroad links, and tweets. Supedia organizes and curates them into a clean, searchable library.
The Problem
I kept wasting time looking for the same types of tools and templates: a good landing page copy file, a Notion business planner, a content calendar, etc. Most of the good stuff was hidden behind paywalls or locked in someone’s link-in-bio. I figured others were facing the same issue.
So I decided to build a solution—start small, focus on quality, and iterate.
What Supedia Is
Supedia is a membership-based resource library. No individual purchases, no upsells. Just a growing vault of digital resources for one monthly price.
There are two memberships:
Digital Resources – $5.95/month
Access to every downloadable PDF, Notion template, marketing kit, and curated resource.
Limitless Pro – $14.95/month
Includes everything in the base plan plus access to exclusive monthly online courses.
Here’s the twist: Limitless Pro members vote on what course we make next—whether it's on content creation, launching a product, building a newsletter, or something else relevant to the digital builder space.
The Build
Solo-built in ~3 months:
Used a simple CMS for uploading and organizing content
Focused on clean UI, mobile-first
Added internal glossaries (SEO-optimized) and creator profiles to boost discovery
Soft-launched on Twitter and in a few niche communities
No code-heavy magic—just curation, structure, and a membership model that felt fair.

500+ downloadable resources (PDFs, templates, toolkits)
Business glossaries for entrepreneurs and marketers
Deep-dive creator profiles (Hormozi, Naval, etc.)
Voting system for course creation (starting April)
What I Learned
Curation is underrated: People don’t want more resources. They want the right ones, clearly presented.
Pricing matters: Offering one low-access tier and one premium tier works better than a complex pricing matrix.
People love having a say: The voting system for Limitless Pro has been more engaging than I expected. Builders want to shape what they learn.
What’s Next
Right now, I’m focused on:
Dropping the first member-voted course (launching late April)
Growing the resource library weekly
Partnering with creators to bring in exclusive content
Still early days, but excited about the direction.
